label: def:measure-mtp2
title: \bf Definition
head: environment
name: Measure-theoretic $\mathrm{MTP}_2$

label: rem:measure-mtp2
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:measure-mtp2}
	\begin{enumerate}
		
		\noindent\item[(i)]
		For $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, define
		$L_{\boldsymbol{x}}:=(-\infty,\boldsymbol{x}]=\prod_{i=1}^d(-\infty,x_i]$.
		Then, for every $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
		$L_{\boldsymbol{x}}\wedge L_{\boldsymbol{y}}=L_{\boldsymbol{x}\wedge\boldsymbol{y}}$ and
		$L_{\boldsymbol{x}}\vee L_{\boldsymbol{y}}=L_{\boldsymbol{x}\vee\boldsymbol{y}}$.
		Consequently, $\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\mu)$ and
		\eqref{eq:measure-mtp2} imply
		$F_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{x})F_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{y})
		\leq
		F_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{x}\wedge\boldsymbol{y})F_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{x}\vee\boldsymbol{y})$,
		where
		$F_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{x}):=\mu(L_{\boldsymbol{x}})$.
		Thus, viewed as the mapping
		$\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto F_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{x})$,
		the distribution function of $\mu$ is $\mathrm{MTP}_2$. The converse does not follow directly from the definition, since
		$\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\mu)$ requires \eqref{eq:measure-mtp2} for all
		admissible pairs $C,D\in\mathcal B_d$, whereas the distribution function tests only the lower orthants $L_{\boldsymbol{x}}$ and $L_{\boldsymbol{y}}$.
		
		\item[(ii)]
		Let $\mu_i:=\mu\circ\pi_i^{-1}$, $i\in[d]$, and set $\nu:=\bigotimes_{i=1}^d\mu_i$. Definition~\ref{def:measure-mtp2} requires neither $\mu\boldsymbol{l}\nu$ nor the existence of a Radon-Nikodym derivative
		$f:=d\mu/d\nu$. If $\mu\boldsymbol{l}\nu$, the usual density-based condition is
		$f(\boldsymbol{x})f(\boldsymbol{y})\leq
		f(\boldsymbol{x}\wedge\boldsymbol{y})f(\boldsymbol{x}\vee\boldsymbol{y})$
		for $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, after choosing a suitable version of $f$. The relation between this pointwise property and
		$\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\mu)$ is not assumed here and will be established under appropriate conditions in Section~\ref{subsec:density-equivalence}.
		In particular, the present construction is meaningful when $\mu\perp\nu$, which is excluded by the density-based formulation in \citet{ColangeloEtAl2006}.
		
		\item[(iii)]
		Define
		$T_{\wedge}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}):=\boldsymbol{x}\wedge\boldsymbol{y}$ and
		$T_{\vee}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}):=\boldsymbol{x}\vee\boldsymbol{y}$ for
		$(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d$.
		Although $T_{\wedge}$ and $T_{\vee}$ are continuous, for
		$C,D\in\mathcal B_d$ the identities
		$C\wedge D=T_{\wedge}(C\times D)$ and
		$C\vee D=T_{\vee}(C\times D)$
		do not guarantee that $C\wedge D$ and $C\vee D$ are Borel. Accordingly, \eqref{eq:measure-mtp2} is imposed only when $C\wedge D,C\vee D\in\mathcal B_d$.The same measurability convention will be used for the conditional
		measure-theoretic formulation introduced in
		Section~\ref{subsec:definition}.
		
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lem:mmtp2-marginal
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mmtp2-marginal}
	If $\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\mu)$ holds, then
	$\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\mu_A)$ holds for every non-empty
	$A\subseteq[d]$.
head: environment
name: Marginal stability

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\varnothing\neq A\subseteq[d]$ and let
	$C,D\in\mathcal B_A$ be such that
	$C\wedge D,C\vee D\in\mathcal B_A$. Set
	$\widetilde C:=\pi_A^{-1}(C)$ and
	$\widetilde D:=\pi_A^{-1}(D)$. Then
	$\widetilde C,\widetilde D\in\mathcal B_d$ and, since the canonical
	projection preserves coordinatewise lattice operations,
	$\widetilde C\wedge\widetilde D
	=\pi_A^{-1}(C\wedge D)$ and
	$\widetilde C\vee\widetilde D
	=\pi_A^{-1}(C\vee D)$.
	Hence, by Definition~\ref{def:measure-mtp2},
	$\mu_A(C)\mu_A(D)
	\leq
	\mu_A(C\wedge D)\mu_A(C\vee D)$.
	Therefore $\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\mu_A)$ holds.
head: environment

label: def:conditional-measure-mtp2
title: \bf Definition
head: environment
name: Conditional measure-theoretic $\mathrm{MTP}_2$

label: rem:conditional-measure-mtp2
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:conditional-measure-mtp2}
	\begin{enumerate}
		
		\noindent \item[(i)]
		Although the notation
		$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ emphasizes the partition $(A,B)$, the property is formulated entirely in terms of the joint
		law $\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol{X}}$. Indeed, if
		$\mu=\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol{X}}$, then \eqref{eq:cmmtp2} is equivalent to
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{split}
				&\mu(C\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B})\mu(D\times L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B})\leq
				\mu((C\wedge D)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B})
				\mu((C\vee D)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}),
			\end{split}
			\label{eq:cmmtp2-joint-law}
		\end{equation}
		for every admissible $C,D\in\mathcal B_A$ and
		$\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B\in\mathbb{R}^B$. More precisely,
		$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ is invariant under the choice of a version of the regular conditional distribution $K_{B\mid A}$.
		
		\item[(ii)]
		For $\boldsymbol{x}_A,\boldsymbol{y}_A\in\mathbb{R}^A$, set
		$C=L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A}$ and $D=L_{\boldsymbol{y}_A}$. Since,
		$L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A}\wedge L_{\boldsymbol{y}_A}=L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_A}$, and
		$L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A}\vee L_{\boldsymbol{y}_A}=L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A\vee\boldsymbol{y}_A}$,
		\eqref{eq:cmmtp2} yields
		$F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}_A,\boldsymbol{x}_B)F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{y}_A,\boldsymbol{y}_B)
		\leq
		F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}_A\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_A,\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B)
		F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}_A\vee\boldsymbol{y}_A,\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B)$. Hence,
		$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ implies
		$\mathrm{MTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$ in the distribution-function sense.
		
		\item[(iii)]
		The conditioning coordinates are not passive in
		\eqref{eq:cmmtp2}. Let $\mathbf t_B=(t_i)_{i\in B}$ with $t_i\uparrow\infty$ for every $i\in B$. Then $L_{\mathbf t_B}\uparrow\mathbb{R}^B$, and continuity from below implies
		$\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\mathbf t_B})
		\to\mu_A(C)$. Invoking \eqref{eq:cmmtp2} with
		$\boldsymbol{x}_B=\boldsymbol{y}_B=\mathbf t_B$ and passing to the limit yields $\mu_A(C)\mu_A(D)\leq
		\mu_A(C\wedge D)\mu_A(C\vee D)$.
		Therefore, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ implies $\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_A)$.
		
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: prop:cmmtp2-finite-measures
title: \bf Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the definition of $\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}^{A}$,
	$\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}^{A}(C)=
	\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B})$.
	Applying the same identity to
	$(\boldsymbol{y}_B,D)$,
	$(\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B,C\wedge D)$, and
	$(\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B,C\vee D)$ shows that
	\eqref{eq:cmmtp2-finite-measures} is precisely
	\eqref{eq:cmmtp2}. The two conditions are therefore equivalent.
head: environment

label: lem:one-dimensional-lattice
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment
name: One-dimensional lattice inequality

title: Proof
body_md:
Equip $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual total order. The constant function
	$h\equiv1$ is $\mathrm{MTP}_2$ with respect to $\lambda$, since
	$h(s)h(t)=h(s\wedge t)h(s\vee t)=1$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$.
	The integral form of the basic composition inequality for
	$\mathrm{MTP}_2$ functions therefore gives
	$\lambda(E)\lambda(F)
	\leq
	\lambda(E\wedge F)\lambda(E\vee F)$
	for every admissible pair $E,F$. Hence the asserted
	measure-theoretic property follows.
head: environment

label: prop:common-factor
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:common-factor}
	Let $Z$ be a real-valued random variable and let
	$\boldsymbol{X}=(g_1(Z),\ldots,g_d(Z))$, where
	$g_i:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $i\in[d]$, are non-decreasing Borel measurable functions \citep{dunbar2026modeling}. Then
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds for every pair of non-empty sets $A,B$ forming a partition of $[d]$.
head: environment
name: Common-factor criterion

label: eq:common-factor-cmmtp2
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\lambda=\mathbb P_Z$ and fix a partition $(A,B)$. For $\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B\in\mathbb{R}^B$ and admissible $C,D\in\mathcal B_A$, define
	$E:=\{z:g_A(z)\in C,\ g_B(z)\leq\boldsymbol{x}_B\}$ and
	$F:=\{z:g_A(z)\in D,\ g_B(z)\leq\boldsymbol{y}_B\}$ \citep{powell2025genomic,pramanik2024analysis}.
	Then $\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}^{A}(C)=\lambda(E)$, and
	$\mu_{\boldsymbol{y}_B}^{A}(D)=\lambda(F)$ \citep{powell2026role,pramanik2026bayesian}. Since every $g_i$ is non-decreasing,
	$g_i(s\wedge t)=g_i(s)\wedge g_i(t)$ and
	$g_i(s\vee t)=g_i(s)\vee g_i(t)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$. Consequently, $E\wedge F$ is contained in $\{z:g_A(z)\in C\wedge D,\
	g_B(z)\leq\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B\}$, where
	$E\vee F$ is contained in
	$\{z:g_A(z)\in C\vee D,\
	g_B(z)\leq\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B\}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:one-dimensional-lattice} therefore yields
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}^{A}(C)\mu_{\boldsymbol{y}_B}^{A}(D)
			&=\lambda(E)\lambda(F)\leq\lambda(E\wedge F)\lambda(E\vee F)\leq
			\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B}^{A}(C\wedge D)
			\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}^{A}(C\vee D).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:common-factor-cmmtp2}
	\end{equation}
	The assertion follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:cmmtp2-finite-measures}.
head: environment

label: ex:comonotonic
title: \bf Example
body_md:
\label{ex:comonotonic}
	Let $U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ and let
	$F_1,\ldots,F_d$ be continuous and strictly increasing distribution functions. Define
	$\boldsymbol{X}=(F_1^{-1}(U),\ldots,F_d^{-1}(U))$.
	Then $\boldsymbol{X}$ is comonotonic and, by
	Proposition~\ref{prop:common-factor},
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds for every pair of non-empty sets $A,B$ forming a partition of $[d]$. On the other hand, the law of $\boldsymbol{X}$ is concentrated on the chain
	$\{(F_1^{-1}(u),\ldots,F_d^{-1}(u)):u\in(0,1)\}$.
	Since the marginal distributions are continuous \citep{pramanik2025dissecting,yusuf2025prognostic}, this set has measure zero under
	$\bigotimes_{i=1}^d\mathbb P_{X_i}$ whenever $d\geq2$. Consequently,
	$\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol{X}}\perp
	\bigotimes_{i=1}^d\mathbb P_{X_i}$,
	so that $\boldsymbol{X}$ does not admit the product-measure density required by the density-based formulation \citep{yusuf2025predictive}. Thus $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2$ applies to this extremal positively dependent model without imposing absolute
	continuity.

label: thm:conditioning-reduction
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:conditioning-reduction}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$, with
	$|A|\geq2$. If $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds, then, for every $k\in A$,
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2
	(\boldsymbol{X}_{B\cup\{k\}}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{A\setminus\{k\}})$ holds.
head: environment
name: Reduction of the conditioning block

label: eq:conditioning-reduction-sets
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $k\in A$ and set $A':=A\setminus\{k\}$ and
	$B':=B\cup\{k\}$. Let $C,D\in\mathcal B_{A'}$ be such that
	$C\wedge D,C\vee D\in\mathcal B_{A'}$, and let
	$\boldsymbol{x}_{B'},\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}\in\mathbb{R}^{B'}$. Write
	$\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}=(\boldsymbol{x}_B,x_k)$ and
	$\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}=(\boldsymbol{y}_B,y_k)$, and define
	$C_x:=C\times(-\infty,x_k]$ and
	$D_y:=D\times(-\infty,y_k]$.
	Then $C_x,D_y\in\mathcal B_A$. We first identify the lattice operations on these sets. By the
	componentwise definition of $\wedge$ and $\vee$,
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			C_x\wedge D_y
			&=(C\wedge D)\times(-\infty,x_k\wedge y_k],\\
			C_x\vee D_y
			&=(C\vee D)\times(-\infty,x_k\vee y_k].
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:conditioning-reduction-sets}
	\end{equation}
	In particular, both sets in
	\eqref{eq:conditioning-reduction-sets} belong to $\mathcal B_A$ \citep{vikramdeo2024mitochondrial}. Hence, $C_x$ and $D_y$ form an admissible pair in
	Definition~\ref{def:conditional-measure-mtp2} \citep{pramanik2024estimation,pramanik2025optimal}. Next observe that
	$\{\boldsymbol{X}_{A'}\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}}\}
	=
	\{\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C_x,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}\}$,
	and analogously
	$\{\boldsymbol{X}_{A'}\in D,\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}}\}
	=
	\{\boldsymbol{X}_A\in D_y,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B}\}$ \citep{valdez2025association,valdez2025exploring}. Since, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds,
	\eqref{eq:cmmtp2} applied to $C_x,D_y,\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B$ gives
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			&\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C_x,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in D_y,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B})\leq
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C_x\wedge D_y,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B})\times
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C_x\vee D_y,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:conditioning-reduction-inequality}
	\end{equation}
Invoking \eqref{eq:conditioning-reduction-sets}, the first probability on the right-hand side of
	\eqref{eq:conditioning-reduction-inequality} equals
	$\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_{A'}\in C\wedge D,
	\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}})$,
	whereas the second equals
	$\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_{A'}\in C\vee D,
	\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}\vee\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}})$. The two probabilities on the left-hand side are similarly
	$\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_{A'}\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}})$ \citep{pramanik2024stochastic}
	and
	$\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_{A'}\in D,\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}})$.
	Consequently, \eqref{eq:conditioning-reduction-inequality} is exactly the defining lattice inequality for
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{A'})$. Since, $C,D$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_{B'},\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}$ were arbitrary, the assertion follows \citep{pramanik2025factors,pramanik2025strategies}.

label: cor:iterated-conditioning-reduction
title: \bf Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:iterated-conditioning-reduction}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$, and suppose that
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds. Then, for every non-empty
	$A'\subseteq A$, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2
	(\boldsymbol{X}_{B\cup(A\setminus A')}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{A'})$ holds.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Enumerate $A\setminus A'=\{k_1,\ldots,k_m\}$. Successive application of Theorem~\ref{thm:conditioning-reduction} to
	$k_1,\ldots,k_m$ yields the assertion.
head: environment

label: ex:singular-gaussian-factor
title: \bf Example
body_md:
\label{ex:singular-gaussian-factor}
	Let $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and define
	$\boldsymbol{X}=(X_1,X_2,X_3):=(Z,2Z,3Z)$. Then $\boldsymbol{X}$ is supported on the one-dimensional subspace
	$\{(z,2z,3z):z\in\mathbb{R}\}$ and is therefore singular with respect to
	$\mathbb P_{X_1}\otimes\mathbb P_{X_2}\otimes\mathbb P_{X_3}$. Nevertheless, Proposition~\ref{prop:common-factor} gives
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(X_3\mid(X_1,X_2))$ \citep{pramanik2023optimal,pramanik2024parametric,pramanik2024bayes}. Taking
	$A=\{1,2\}$, $B=\{3\}$, and $k=2$ in
	Theorem~\ref{thm:conditioning-reduction} therefore yields $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2((X_2,X_3)\mid X_1)$. To illustrate the latter property numerically, let
	$C=[-1,1/2]$, $D=[0,3/2]$,
	$\boldsymbol{x}_B=(1,2)$, and $\boldsymbol{y}_B=(2,1)$, where
	$B=\{2,3\}$ \citep{pramanik2023path1}. Since, $C\wedge D=[-1,1/2]$ and $C\vee D=[0,3/2]$, while $\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B=(1,1)$ and
	$\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B=(2,2)$, we obtain
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			\mathbb P(X_1\in C,(X_2,X_3)\leq\boldsymbol{x}_B)
			\mathbb P(X_1\in D,(X_2,X_3)\leq\boldsymbol{y}_B)
			&=
			\mathbb P(-1\leq Z\leq1/2)
			\mathbb P(0\leq Z\leq1/3)\\
			&\approx
			(0.5328)(0.1306)
			=
			0.0696,
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:singular-gaussian-left}
	\end{equation}
	whereas
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			\mathbb P(X_1\in C\wedge D,
			(X_2,X_3)\leq\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B)
			&\times
			\mathbb P(X_1\in C\vee D,
			(X_2,X_3)\leq\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B)\\
			&=
			\mathbb P(-1\leq Z\leq1/3)
			\mathbb P(0\leq Z\leq2/3)\approx
			(0.4719)(0.2475)
			=
			0.1168.
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:singular-gaussian-right}
	\end{equation}
	Hence, the lattice inequality is strict for this choice of $C,D,\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B$, since $0.0696<0.1168$.

label: def:cmmtp2-vector
title: \bf Definition
body_md:
\label{def:cmmtp2-vector}
	A $d$-dimensional random vector $\boldsymbol{X}$ is said to be
	conditionally measure-theoretically multivariate totally positive of order two, and we write $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$, if
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds for every pair of non-empty
	sets $A,B$ forming a partition of $[d]$.
head: environment

label: thm:cmmtp2-marginalization
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cmmtp2-marginalization}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$. For a
	$d$-dimensional random vector $\boldsymbol{X}$, we have:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)]
		If $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds, then
		$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{A'})$ holds for all non-empty
		$A'\subseteq A$ and $B'\subseteq B$.
		
		\item[(ii)]
		If $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$ holds, then
		$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_I)$ holds for every
		$I\subseteq[d]$ with $|I|\geq2$.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: eq:conditioned-marginalization
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove (i). Suppose that
$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds. We begin with
marginalization in the conditioned block. The argument follows the usual marginalization principle for $\mathrm{MTP}_2$ measures, but is applied here to the mixed set-orthant formulation in
Definition~\ref{def:conditional-measure-mtp2}
\citep{ColangeloEtAl2006,FallatEtAl2017}.
Let $\varnothing\neq B'\subseteq B$ and set $J:=B\setminus B'$. Fix $\boldsymbol{x}_{B'},\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}\in\mathbb{R}^{B'}$ and admissible
$C,D\in\mathcal B_A$. For $n\geq1$, define
$\boldsymbol{x}_B^{(n)},\boldsymbol{y}_B^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^B$ by
$\boldsymbol{x}_B^{(n)}=(\boldsymbol{x}_{B'},n\boldsymbol{1}_J)$ and
$\boldsymbol{y}_B^{(n)}=(\boldsymbol{y}_{B'},n\boldsymbol{1}_J)$,
where $\boldsymbol{1}_J$ denotes the vector of ones indexed by $J$.
Definition~\ref{def:conditional-measure-mtp2} gives
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			&\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B^{(n)}})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in D,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B^{(n)}})\\
			&\hspace{1cm}\leq
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C\wedge D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B^{(n)}\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B^{(n)}})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C\vee D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B^{(n)}\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B^{(n)}}).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:conditioned-marginalization}
	\end{equation}
	Since $n\to\infty$, the four events in
	\eqref{eq:conditioned-marginalization} increase, respectively, to the
	corresponding events involving only $\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}$. Continuity from below
	therefore yields
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			&\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in D,\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}})\\
			&\hspace{1cm}\leq
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C\wedge D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C\vee D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_{B'}\vee\boldsymbol{y}_{B'}}).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:conditioned-marginal-limit}
	\end{equation}
	Hence, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds. Now let $\varnothing\neq A'\subseteq A$ and set
	$K:=A\setminus A'$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-conditioning-reduction},
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_{B\cup K}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{A'})$ holds \citep{issah2026stochastic,pramanik2026viscosity,pramanik2026stochastic}. Applying the conditioned-block marginalization just proved, first retaining $B$ and then $B'\subseteq
	B$, yields $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{A'})$. This proves (i). We now prove (ii). Suppose $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$ holds and fix
	$I\subseteq[d]$ with $|I|\geq2$. Let $A'$ and $B'$ be arbitrary non-empty sets forming a partition of $I$. Define $A:=A'\cup I^c$ and $B:=B'$. Then $A$ and $B$ form a partition of
	$[d]$, and Definition~\ref{def:cmmtp2-vector} yields
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$. Applying part (i) with $A'\subseteq A$ gives
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_{B'}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{A'})$. Since the partition	$(A',B')$ of $I$ was arbitrary,
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_I)$ follows from
	Definition~\ref{def:cmmtp2-vector}. This proves (ii).

label: thm:basic-implications
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:basic-implications}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$. For a
	$d$-dimensional random vector $\boldsymbol{X}$, we have:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)]
		$\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$ implies
		$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$.
		
		\item[(ii)]
		$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ implies
		$\mathrm{MTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: eq:product-set-lattice
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove (i). Let $\mu=\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol{X}}$ and suppose that
	$\mathrm{mMTP}_2(\mu)$ holds. Fix
	$\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B\in\mathbb{R}^B$ and
	$C,D\in\mathcal B_A$ such that
	$C\wedge D,C\vee D\in\mathcal B_A$. Define
	$E:=C\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}$ and
	$F:=D\times L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B}$. Then $E,F\in\mathcal B_d$, and the
	componentwise lattice operations give
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			E\wedge F
			&=(C\wedge D)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B},\
			\ E\vee F
			=(C\vee D)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}.
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:product-set-lattice}
	\end{equation}
	Hence $E\wedge F,E\vee F\in\mathcal B_d$ \citep{pramanik2022lock,pramanik2022stochastic}. Applying
	Definition~\ref{def:measure-mtp2} to $E$ and $F$ yields
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			&\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in D,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B})\leq
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C\wedge D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{X}_A\in C\vee D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:mmtp2-implies-cmmtp2}
	\end{equation}
	Since $C,D,\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B$ were arbitrary \citep{pramanik2024dependence,pramanik2024measuring},
	\eqref{eq:mmtp2-implies-cmmtp2} is precisely
	\eqref{eq:cmmtp2} \citep{pramanik2021consensus,pramanik2021optimization}. Therefore, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds. We now prove (ii). Suppose
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds \citep{pramanik2016tail}. For
	$\boldsymbol{x}=(\boldsymbol{x}_A,\boldsymbol{x}_B)$, and
	$\boldsymbol{y}=(\boldsymbol{y}_A,\boldsymbol{y}_B)$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, take
	$C=L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A}$ and $D=L_{\boldsymbol{y}_A}$ in
	Definition~\ref{def:conditional-measure-mtp2}. Since,
	$L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A}\wedge L_{\boldsymbol{y}_A}=L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_A}$ and
	$L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A}\vee L_{\boldsymbol{y}_A}=L_{\boldsymbol{x}_A\vee\boldsymbol{y}_A}$, we obtain $F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x})F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{y})\leq
	F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}\wedge\boldsymbol{y})F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}\vee\boldsymbol{y})$.
	Hence, the mapping $\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ is $\mathrm{MTP}_2$, which proves $\mathrm{MTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$.

label: lem:cmmtp2-determining-class
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cmmtp2-determining-class}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$.
	Then $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds if and only if
	\eqref{eq:cmmtp2} holds for all $\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B\in\mathbb{R}^B$ and all
	strongly disjoint noncomparable closed rectangles $C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^A$.
head: environment
name: Determining class

title: Proof
body_md:
Necessity is immediate. For the converse, let $\mathcal I_A$ be the
	class of half-open rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^A$ and set
	$\mathcal A_A:=\operatorname{alg}(\mathcal I_A)$. For
	$C,D\in\mathcal A_A$, choose a common finite rectangular partition
	$(R_j)_{j\in J}$ such that
	$C=\dot\bigcup_{j\in J_C}R_j$ and
	$D=\dot\bigcup_{j\in J_D}R_j$. The assumed inequality on strongly disjoint noncomparable rectangles, together with the finite lattice inequality, yields
	\eqref{eq:cmmtp2} for $C,D\in\mathcal A_A$. Fix $\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B\in\mathbb{R}^B$ and define
	$\alpha:=\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}^{A}$,
	$\beta:=\mu_{\boldsymbol{y}_B}^{A}$,
	$\gamma:=\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B}^{A}$, and
	$\delta:=\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}^{A}$. For $D\in\mathcal A_A$, let
	$\mathcal G_D:=\{C\in\mathcal B_A:
	\alpha(C)\beta(D)\leq
	\gamma(C\wedge D)\delta(C\vee D)\}$.
	Then $\mathcal A_A\subseteq\mathcal G_D$, and continuity under monotone limits gives that $\mathcal G_D$ is a monotone class.
	Hence $\mathcal G_D=\mathcal B_A$. Similarly, for
	$C\in\mathcal B_A$, define
	$\mathcal H_C:=\{D\in\mathcal B_A:
	\alpha(C)\beta(D)\leq
	\gamma(C\wedge D)\delta(C\vee D)\}$.
	Again $\mathcal A_A\subseteq\mathcal H_C$ and
	$\mathcal H_C$ is a monotone class, so
	$\mathcal H_C=\mathcal B_A$. Proposition~\ref{prop:cmmtp2-finite-measures}
	now gives $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$.

label: thm:cmmtp2-weak-closure
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cmmtp2-weak-closure}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$, and
	let $\mu_n,\mu$ be probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. Suppose
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2((\boldsymbol{X}_n)_B\mid(\boldsymbol{X}_n)_A)$ holds for every $n$, where $\boldsymbol{X}_n\sim\mu_n$. Then
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds for $\boldsymbol{X}\sim\mu$.
head: environment

label: eq:weak-continuity-approximation
title: Proof
head: environment

label: rem:weak-closure
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:weak-closure}
	Theorem~\ref{thm:cmmtp2-weak-closure} requires neither $\mu_n\boldsymbol{l}\lambda_d$ nor $\mu\boldsymbol{l}\lambda_d$. Thus it may happen that
	$\mu_n\boldsymbol{l}\lambda_d$ for every $n$, while
	$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ and $\mu\perp\lambda_d$. More precisely, $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ and
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2((\boldsymbol{X}_n)_B\mid(\boldsymbol{X}_n)_A)$ for every $n$ imply $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ even when $\mu$ is singular. Moreover, under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:cmtp2-to-cmmtp2},
	$\mathrm{cMTP}_2((\boldsymbol{X}_n)_B\mid(\boldsymbol{X}_n)_A)$ implies
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2((\boldsymbol{X}_n)_B\mid(\boldsymbol{X}_n)_A)$. Hence, the weak limit retains the measure theoretic conditional property even when a density-based approach is unavailable at $\mu$.
head: environment

label: ex:weak-gaussian-limit
title: \bf Example
body_md:
\label{ex:weak-gaussian-limit}
	Let $Z,E_1,E_2$ be independent standard normal random variables and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define
	$X_{\varepsilon}:=Z+\varepsilon E_1$ and
	$Y_{\varepsilon}:=Z+\varepsilon E_2$. Then
	$(X_{\varepsilon},Y_{\varepsilon})\sim
	\mathcal N(\boldsymbol{0},\Sigma_{\varepsilon})$, where
	\begin{equation}
		\Sigma_{\varepsilon}
		=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			1+\varepsilon^2 & 1\\
			1 & 1+\varepsilon^2
		\end{pmatrix},
		\qquad
		\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}
		=
		\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2(2+\varepsilon^2)}
		\begin{pmatrix}
			1+\varepsilon^2 & -1\\
			-1 & 1+\varepsilon^2
		\end{pmatrix}.
		\label{eq:gaussian-weak-example}
	\end{equation}
	Hence, $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}$ is an $M$-matrix and $(X_{\varepsilon},Y_{\varepsilon})$ is $\mathrm{dMTP}_2$ for every
	$\varepsilon>0$ \citep{FallatEtAl2017}. In particular, Theorem~\ref{thm:basic-implications}(i) yields $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(Y_{\varepsilon}\mid X_{\varepsilon})$. Consider $\varepsilon\in\{1,1/2,1/5,1/10\}$. The
	correlations are
	\begin{center}
		\begin{tabular}{c|cccc}
			$\varepsilon$
			& $1$ & $1/2$ & $1/5$ & $1/10$\\ \hline
			$\operatorname{Corr}(X_{\varepsilon},Y_{\varepsilon})$
			& $0.5000$ & $0.8000$ & $0.9615$ & $0.9901$
		\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
	and therefore converge to $1$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The corresponding lower-orthant probabilities provide a direct
	probability-level illustration of the convergence. Since
	$\rho_{\varepsilon}:=
	\operatorname{Corr}(X_{\varepsilon},Y_{\varepsilon})
	=(1+\varepsilon^2)^{-1}$, the bivariate Gaussian orthant formula gives
	$\mathbb P(X_{\varepsilon}\leq0,Y_{\varepsilon}\leq0)
	=1/4+(2\pi)^{-1}\arcsin(\rho_{\varepsilon})$. Hence,
	
	\begin{center}
		\begin{tabular}{c|cccc}
			$\varepsilon$
			& $1$ & $1/2$ & $1/5$ & $1/10$\\ \hline
			$\mathbb P(X_{\varepsilon}\leq0,Y_{\varepsilon}\leq0)$
			& $0.3333$ & $0.3976$ & $0.4557$ & $0.4776$
		\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
	
	\noindent As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, $\rho_{\varepsilon}\uparrow1$ and
	therefore,
	$\mathbb P(X_{\varepsilon}\leq0,Y_{\varepsilon}\leq0)\to1/2$.
	For the limiting vector $(Z,Z)$,
	$\mathbb P(Z\leq0,Z\leq0)=\mathbb P(Z\leq0)=1/2$.	Moreover,
	$(X_{\varepsilon},Y_{\varepsilon})\Rightarrow(Z,Z)$.
	The limiting distribution is concentrated on
	$\{(z,z):z\in\mathbb{R}\}$, and hence is singular with respect to $\mathbb P_Z\otimes\mathbb P_Z$. Taking $A=\{1\}$ and $B=\{2\}$, Theorem~\ref{thm:cmmtp2-weak-closure} implies
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(Z\mid Z)$ for the limiting random vector $(Z,Z)$. Therefore, every member of the approximating family admits a
	strictly positive Gaussian density, whereas the limit has no density with respect to the product of its marginals. Nevertheless, the conditional measure theoretic total positivity property is preserved.

label: lem:monotone-lattice-map
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:monotone-lattice-map}
	Suppose $\phi_i:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $i\in I$, are strictly increasing Borel functions. Then, for $\boldsymbol{x}_I,\boldsymbol{y}_I\in\mathbb{R}^I$,
	$\phi_I(\boldsymbol{x}_I\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_I)
	=\phi_I(\boldsymbol{x}_I)\wedge\phi_I(\boldsymbol{y}_I)$ and
	$\phi_I(\boldsymbol{x}_I\vee\boldsymbol{y}_I)
	=\phi_I(\boldsymbol{x}_I)\vee\phi_I(\boldsymbol{y}_I)$.
	Moreover, for admissible Borel sets
	$C,D\subseteq\phi_I(\mathbb{R}^I)$,
	$\phi_I^{-1}(C\wedge D)
	=\phi_I^{-1}(C)\wedge\phi_I^{-1}(D)$ and
	$\phi_I^{-1}(C\vee D)
	=\phi_I^{-1}(C)\vee\phi_I^{-1}(D)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $i\in I$, strict monotonicity gives
	$\phi_i(x_i\wedge y_i)
	=\phi_i(x_i)\wedge\phi_i(y_i)$ and
	$\phi_i(x_i\vee y_i)
	=\phi_i(x_i)\vee\phi_i(y_i)$.
	The vector identities follow coordinatewise. Applying them to
	$\boldsymbol{x}_I\in\phi_I^{-1}(C)$ and
	$\boldsymbol{y}_I\in\phi_I^{-1}(D)$, and using injectivity of $\phi_I$, gives the two inverse-image identities.
head: environment

label: lem:lower-ray-extension
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lower-ray-extension}
	If $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds, then its defining
	inequality remains valid when $L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B}$ and $L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B}$ are
	replaced by arbitrary coordinatewise lower rays, with intersection
	and union in the corresponding lattice terms.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For lower rays $H_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, choose
	$a_i^{(m)}$ such that
	$(-\infty,a_i^{(m)}]\uparrow H_i$. Hence, with
	$\boldsymbol{a}_B^{(m)}:=(a_i^{(m)})_{i\in B}$,
	$L_{\boldsymbol{a}_B^{(m)}}\uparrow\prod_{i\in B}H_i$.
	Apply Definition~\ref{def:conditional-measure-mtp2} and let
	$m\to\infty$. Continuity from below, together with
	$(H_i\cap G_i)$ and $(H_i\cup G_i)$ being lower rays, gives the
	assertion.
head: environment

label: prop:monotone-transformations
title: \bf Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:inverse-lattice-transform
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove (i). Write
	$\phi_A(\boldsymbol{x}_A):=(\phi_i(x_i))_{i\in A}$ and let
	$C,D\in\mathcal B_A$ be admissible for $\boldsymbol{Y}_A$. Since
	$\boldsymbol{Y}_A\in\phi_A(\mathbb{R}^A)$ almost surely, we may replace $C,D$ by
	$C\cap\phi_A(\mathbb{R}^A)$ and $D\cap\phi_A(\mathbb{R}^A)$, respectively.
	Set
	$C':=\phi_A^{-1}(C)$ and $D':=\phi_A^{-1}(D)$.
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:monotone-lattice-map},
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			C'\wedge D'&=\phi_A^{-1}(C\wedge D),\ \
			C'\vee D'=\phi_A^{-1}(C\vee D).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:inverse-lattice-transform}
	\end{equation}
	Fix $\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B\in\mathbb{R}^B$. Applying
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ to
	$C',D',\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B$ and using
	$\{\boldsymbol{Y}_A\in E\}=\{\boldsymbol{X}_A\in\phi_A^{-1}(E)\}$ gives
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			&\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{Y}_A\in C,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{Y}_A\in D,\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B})\leq
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{Y}_A\in C\wedge D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B})
			\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{Y}_A\in C\vee D,
			\boldsymbol{X}_B\in L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:transform-conditioning-block}
	\end{equation}
	Therefore, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{Y}_A)$ holds.
	We now prove (ii). For $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $i\in B$, set
	$H_i(t):=\{s\in\mathbb{R}:\phi_i(s)\leq t\}$. Since $\phi_i$ is strictly
	increasing, $H_i(t)$ is a lower ray and, for $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$,
	$H_i(s\wedge t)=H_i(s)\cap H_i(t)$ and
	$H_i(s\vee t)=H_i(s)\cup H_i(t)$. Hence, for
	$\boldsymbol{x}_B\in\mathbb{R}^B$,
	\begin{equation}
		\{\boldsymbol{Y}_B\leq\boldsymbol{x}_B\}
		=
		\{\boldsymbol{X}_B\in H_B(\boldsymbol{x}_B)\},
		\qquad
		H_B(\boldsymbol{x}_B):=\prod_{i\in B}H_i(x_i).
		\label{eq:lower-ray-preimage}
	\end{equation}
	For admissible $C,D\in\mathcal B_A$, apply
	Lemma~\ref{lem:lower-ray-extension} to
	$H_B(\boldsymbol{x}_B)$ and $H_B(\boldsymbol{y}_B)$. Since
	$H_B(\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B)
	=H_B(\boldsymbol{x}_B)\cap H_B(\boldsymbol{y}_B)$ and
	$H_B(\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B)
	=H_B(\boldsymbol{x}_B)\cup H_B(\boldsymbol{y}_B)$ coordinatewise, part (i) yields the
	defining inequality for
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{Y}_B\mid\boldsymbol{Y}_A)$.
head: environment

label: thm:monotone-transformations
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:monotone-transformations}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$ and
	suppose $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds. Let
	$\phi_i:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $i\in[d]$, be non-decreasing Borel functions and
	define $Y_i:=\phi_i(X_i)$. Then
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{Y}_B\mid\boldsymbol{Y}_A)$ holds.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $n\geq1$, define
	$\phi_i^{(n)}(x):=\phi_i(x)+x/n$ and
	$Y_i^{(n)}:=\phi_i^{(n)}(X_i)$. Each $\phi_i^{(n)}$ is strictly increasing, so Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone-transformations}(ii)
	gives $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{Y}_B^{(n)}\mid\boldsymbol{Y}_A^{(n)})$.
	Moreover, $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(n)}\to\boldsymbol{Y}$ almost surely and hence,
	$\boldsymbol{Y}^{(n)}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{Y}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:cmmtp2-weak-closure}
	therefore yields $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{Y}_B\mid\boldsymbol{Y}_A)$.
head: environment

label: cor:monotone-transformations-vector
title: \bf Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:monotone-transformations-vector}
	Suppose $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$ holds and let
	$\phi_i:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $i\in[d]$, be non-decreasing Borel functions. Then
	$\phi(\boldsymbol{X}):=(\phi_1(X_1),\ldots,\phi_d(X_d))$
	is $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every non-trivial partition $(A,B)$ of $[d]$,
	Definition~\ref{def:cmmtp2-vector} and
	Theorem~\ref{thm:monotone-transformations} give
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\phi_B(\boldsymbol{X}_B)\mid\phi_A(\boldsymbol{X}_A))$.
	Hence $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\phi(\boldsymbol{X}))$.
head: environment

label: ex:monotone-thresholding
title: \bf Example
body_md:
\label{ex:monotone-thresholding}
	Let $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and
	$\boldsymbol{X}=(Z,2Z,3Z)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:common-factor},
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$ holds. Define
	$\phi_i(x):=\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}}$, $i\in[3]$, and
	$\boldsymbol{Y}:=\phi(\boldsymbol{X})$. Then $\boldsymbol{Y}=(I,I,I)$, where
	$I:=\mathbf 1_{\{Z>0\}}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$.

	Corollary~\ref{cor:monotone-transformations-vector} yields
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{Y})$. For $A=\{1,2\}$, $B=\{3\}$,
	$C=\{(0,0)\}$, $D=\{(1,1)\}$, $x_3=0$, and $y_3=1$,
	the two sides of \eqref{eq:cmmtp2} are both
	$(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$.

label: lem:kernel-integration
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment
name: Lattice-positive kernel integration

title: Proof
body_md:
Put
	$f_1(\boldsymbol{u}_B):=H(\boldsymbol{u}_B,L_{\boldsymbol{x}_C})$,
	$f_2(\boldsymbol{v}_B):=H(\boldsymbol{v}_B,L_{\boldsymbol{y}_C})$,
	$f_3(\boldsymbol{w}_B):=H(\boldsymbol{w}_B,L_{\boldsymbol{x}_C\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_C})$, and
	$f_4(\boldsymbol{z}_B):=H(\boldsymbol{z}_B,L_{\boldsymbol{x}_C\vee\boldsymbol{y}_C})$.
	Since $H\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{LTP}_2}(B,C)$,
	$f_1(\boldsymbol{u}_B)f_2(\boldsymbol{v}_B)
	\leq f_3(\boldsymbol{u}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{v}_B)f_4(\boldsymbol{u}_B\vee\boldsymbol{v}_B)$.
	Set
	$K_1:=K(\boldsymbol{x}_A,\cdot)$,
	$K_2:=K(\boldsymbol{y}_A,\cdot)$,
	$K_3:=K(\boldsymbol{x}_A\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_A,\cdot)$, and
	$K_4:=K(\boldsymbol{x}_A\vee\boldsymbol{y}_A,\cdot)$.
	By \eqref{eq:measure-lattice-positive-kernel},
	$K_1(E)K_2(F)\leq K_3(E\wedge F)K_4(E\vee F)$ for every admissible $E,F\in\mathcal B_B$. The integral four-functions inequality \citep{KarlinRinott1980a} now yields $(\int f_1\,dK_1)(\int f_2\,dK_2)
	\leq(\int f_3\,dK_3)(\int f_4\,dK_4)$, which is
	\eqref{eq:kernel-integration}. This completes the proof.

label: rem:conditional-independence-kernels
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:conditional-independence-kernels}
	Let $(\boldsymbol{X}_A,\boldsymbol{X}_B,\boldsymbol{X}_C)$ have distribution
	\begin{equation}
		\mathbb P(d\boldsymbol{x}_A,d\boldsymbol{x}_B,d\boldsymbol{x}_C)
		=
		\lambda(d\boldsymbol{x}_A)
		K_1(\boldsymbol{x}_A,d\boldsymbol{x}_B)
		K_2(\boldsymbol{x}_B,d\boldsymbol{x}_C).
		\label{eq:markov-factorization}
	\end{equation}
	Then $\boldsymbol{X}_A\perp\boldsymbol{X}_C\mid\boldsymbol{X}_B$, and the conditional kernel of
	$\boldsymbol{X}_C$ given $\boldsymbol{X}_A=\boldsymbol{x}_A$ is
	\begin{equation}
		K_{C\mid A}(\boldsymbol{x}_A,E)
		=
		(K_1K_2)(\boldsymbol{x}_A,E)
		=
		\int_{\mathbb{R}^B}K_2(\boldsymbol{x}_B,E)K_1(\boldsymbol{x}_A,d\boldsymbol{x}_B).
		\label{eq:conditional-markov-kernel}
	\end{equation}
	While $\boldsymbol{X}_A\perp\boldsymbol{X}_C\mid\boldsymbol{X}_B$ yields
	\eqref{eq:markov-factorization}, it does not by itself imply $K_{C\mid A}\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{LTP}_2}(A,C)$. By
	Proposition~\ref{prop:kernel-composition},
	$K_1\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{mLTP}_2}(A,B)$ and
	$K_2\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{LTP}_2}(B,C)$ imply
	$K_{C\mid A}=K_1K_2\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{LTP}_2}(A,C)$. Thus, for multivariate $\boldsymbol{X}_B$, kernel positivity supplements
	$\boldsymbol{X}_A\perp\boldsymbol{X}_C\mid\boldsymbol{X}_B$ compared with \citet{FuchsWang2027}.

\label{ex:binary-markov-product}

	$X_1-X_2-X_3$, with
	$\mathbb P(X_1=0)=\mathbb P(X_1=1)=1/2$ and transition kernels
	\begin{center}
		\begin{tabular}{c|cc}
			& $X_2=0$ & $X_2=1$\\ \hline
			$X_1=0$ & $0.8$ & $0.2$\\
			$X_1=1$ & $0.3$ & $0.7$

		\begin{tabular}{c|cc}
			& $X_3=0$ & $X_3=1$\\ \hline
			$X_2=0$ & $0.9$ & $0.1$\\
			$X_2=1$ & $0.4$ & $0.6$

	Take $A=\{1\}$, $B=\{2\}$, and $C=\{3\}$.
	
	\textit{(i)}
	Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ denote the two kernels above. Since the state
	spaces are binary,
	$
	K_1(0,0)K_1(1,1)=0.56>0.06
	=K_1(0,1)K_1(1,0),
	$
	and
	$
	K_2(0,0)K_2(1,1)=0.54>0.04
	=K_2(0,1)K_2(1,0).
	$
	Therefore, $K_1$ and $K_2$ satisfy the corresponding lattice-positive inequalities. In particular,
	$K_1\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{mLTP}_2}(A,B)$ and
	$K_2\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{LTP}_2}(B,C)$.
	
	\textit{(ii)}
	By \eqref{eq:kernel-composition}, the Markov product is
	\begin{equation}
		K_1K_2
		=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			0.8&0.2\\
			0.3&0.7
		\end{pmatrix}
		\begin{pmatrix}
			0.9&0.1\\
			0.4&0.6
		\end{pmatrix}
		=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			0.80&0.20\\
			0.55&0.45
		\end{pmatrix}.
		\label{eq:binary-markov-product}
	\end{equation}
	Hence,
	$\mathbb P(X_3=0\mid X_1=0)=0.80$ and
	$\mathbb P(X_3=0\mid X_1=1)=0.55$, while
	$\mathbb P(X_3\leq1\mid X_1=i)=1$, $i\in\{0,1\}$.

	$0.80(0.45)=0.36>0.11=0.20(0.55)$, so that
	$K_1K_2\in\mathcal K_{\mathrm{LTP}_2}(A,C)$, in agreement with
	Proposition~\ref{prop:kernel-composition}. Finally, since $\lambda=(1/2,1/2)$ is

	\mathbb P(X_1\in E,X_3\leq0)
	\mathbb P(X_1\in F,X_3\leq1)
	=(0.40)(0.50)=0.20,

	\mathbb P(X_1\in E\wedge F,X_3\leq0)
	\mathbb P(X_1\in E\vee F,X_3\leq1)

body_md:
\label{prop:copula-invariance}
	Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty sets forming a partition of $[d]$.
	Suppose that $F_i$, $i\in[d]$, are continuous and strictly
	increasing, and set $U_i:=F_i(X_i)$. Then

head: environment
name: Copula invariance

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds. Since each
	$F_i$ is non-decreasing, Theorem~\ref{thm:monotone-transformations}
	yields
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)$. Conversely, let $Q_i:=F_i^{-1}$, $i\in[d]$. Since, $F_i$ is
	continuous and strictly increasing, $Q_i$ is strictly increasing and
	$X_i=Q_i(U_i)$ almost surely. Hence
	Theorem~\ref{thm:monotone-transformations}, applied to $\boldsymbol{U}$ and $(Q_i)_{i\in[d]}$, yields
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$.

label: thm:archimedean-cmmtp2
title: \bf Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:archimedean-conditional-map
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $U_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$, $i\in A$, we have
	$\nu_A=\bigotimes_{i\in A}\mathbb P_{U_i}
	=\lambda^k|_{(0,1)^k}$, whose density is strictly positive and
	continuous. Hence, under the stated regularity assumptions,
	Theorem~\ref{thm:density-equivalence} gives
	$
	\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)
	\Longleftrightarrow
	\mathrm{cMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A).
	$
	It remains to prove $(ii)\Longleftrightarrow(iii)$.
	For $\boldsymbol{u}_A\in(0,1)^k$ and $\boldsymbol{u}_B\in(0,1]^{d-k}$,
	differentiating \eqref{eq:archimedean-copula} with respect to $\boldsymbol{u}_A$ yields
	\begin{equation}
		\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{U}_B\leq\boldsymbol{u}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A=\boldsymbol{u}_A)c_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A)
		=
		h_k\!\left(s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B)\right)
		\prod_{i\in A}\{-\varphi'(u_i)\},
		\label{eq:archimedean-conditional-map}
	\end{equation}
	where
	$c_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A)
	=h_k(s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A))
	\prod_{i\in A}\{-\varphi'(u_i)\}$.
	Therefore, the mapping defining $\mathrm{cMTP}_2$ is
	$$
	g(\boldsymbol{u}_A,\boldsymbol{u}_B)
	=
	h_k\!\left(s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B)\right)
	\prod_{i\in A}\{-\varphi'(u_i)\}.
	$$
	The product factor is lattice-neutral, since, for
	$\boldsymbol{u}_A,\boldsymbol{v}_A\in(0,1)^k$,
	\[
	\prod_{i\in A}\{-\varphi'(u_i)\}
	\prod_{i\in A}\{-\varphi'(v_i)\}
	=
	\prod_{i\in A}\{-\varphi'(u_i\wedge v_i)\}
	\prod_{i\in A}\{-\varphi'(u_i\vee v_i)\}.
	\]
Consequently, the $\mathrm{MTP}_2$ inequality for $g$ reduces to
\begin{equation}
	\begin{split}
		h_k\!\left(s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B)\right)
		h_k\!\left(s_A(\boldsymbol{v}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{v}_B)\right)&\leq
		h_k\!\left(s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A\wedge\boldsymbol{v}_A)
		+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{v}_B)\right)\\
		&\hspace{1cm}\times
		h_k\!\left(s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A\vee\boldsymbol{v}_A)
		+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B\vee\boldsymbol{v}_B)\right).
	\end{split}
	\label{eq:archimedean-hk-lattice}
\end{equation}
Since $\varphi$ is decreasing,
$s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A\vee\boldsymbol{v}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B\vee\boldsymbol{v}_B)
\leq
\min\{r,s\}\leq
\max\{r,s\}\leq
s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A\wedge\boldsymbol{v}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{v}_B)$,
where
$r:=s_A(\boldsymbol{u}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{u}_B)$ and
$s:=s_A(\boldsymbol{v}_A)+s_B(\boldsymbol{v}_B)$, while the sums of the two extreme arguments and of $r,s$ coincide. Hence,
\eqref{eq:archimedean-hk-lattice} is equivalent to convexity of
$\log h_k$ \citep{MullerScarsini2005,FuchsWang2027}. Thus
$(ii)\Longleftrightarrow(iii)$, and the assertion follows. Combining this with
	$(i)\Longleftrightarrow(ii)$ proves the assertion.

label: cor:clayton-cmmtp2
title: \bf Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:clayton-cmmtp2}
	Let $\boldsymbol{U}$ have the $d$-dimensional Clayton copula with parameter
	$\theta>0$. Then, for every non-trivial partition $(A,B)$ of
	$[d]$,
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)$ holds.
head: environment
name: Clayton copulas

label: eq:clayton-hk
title: Proof
body_md:
For $\theta>0$, the Clayton generator is
	$\psi_\theta(t)=(1+t)^{-1/\theta}$. If $|A|=k$, then
	\begin{equation}
		h_k(t)
		=
		(-1)^k\psi_\theta^{(k)}(t)
		=
		\left\{\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}
		\left(\frac{1}{\theta}+j\right)\right\}
		(1+t)^{-1/\theta-k}.
		\label{eq:clayton-hk}
	\end{equation}
	Hence,
	$(\log h_k)''(t)=(1/\theta+k)(1+t)^{-2}>0$ for $t>0$.
	Therefore, $h_k$ is log-convex, and
	Theorem~\ref{thm:archimedean-cmmtp2} yields
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)$.

label: thm:gaussian-cmmtp2
title: \bf Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:gaussian-conditional-hessian
title: Proof
body_md:
By Gaussian conditioning,
	$\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A=\boldsymbol{x}_A\sim
	N_{|B|}(\boldsymbol\mu_B+
	M(\boldsymbol{x}_A-\boldsymbol\mu_A),V)$.
	Thus, with
	$\boldsymbol{z}:=\boldsymbol{x}_B-\boldsymbol\mu_B-
	M(\boldsymbol{x}_A-\boldsymbol\mu_A)$,
	the conditional map in Theorem~
	\ref{thm:density-equivalence} is
	$g(\boldsymbol{x}_A,\boldsymbol{x}_B)=f_A(\boldsymbol{x}_A)\Phi_V(\boldsymbol{z})$.
	Since $g>0$ and $g\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$,
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$
	is equivalent to
	$\partial_{ij}^2\log g\geq0$ for all
	$i\neq j$, by Theorem~
	\ref{thm:density-equivalence}
	and the differential criterion for
	$\mathrm{MTP}_2$. Direct differentiation gives
	\begin{equation}
		\nabla^2\log g=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			-S+M^\top H(\boldsymbol{z})M&-M^\top H(\boldsymbol{z})\\
			-H(\boldsymbol{z})M&H(\boldsymbol{z})
		\end{pmatrix}.
		\label{eq:gaussian-conditional-hessian}
	\end{equation}
	Nonnegativity of its off-diagonal
	entries is precisely
	\eqref{eq:gaussian-conditional-criterion},
	proving both directions.

label: cor:gaussian-singleton
title: \bf Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:gaussian-singleton}
	Let $\boldsymbol{X}\sim N_d(\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma)$, $\Sigma\succ0$,
	and $A=[d]\setminus\{b\}$, $B=\{b\}$. Set
	$S:=\Sigma_{AA}^{-1}$,
	$\boldsymbol\beta:=\Sigma_{bA}\Sigma_{AA}^{-1}$,
	and $v:=\Sigma_{bb}-\Sigma_{bA}
	\Sigma_{AA}^{-1}\Sigma_{Ab}>0$.
	Then $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(X_b\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ holds if and
	only if
	\begin{equation}
		S_{ij}+\frac{\beta_i\beta_j}{v}\leq0,
		\ i\neq j,\ i,j\in A,
		\qquad
		\beta_i\geq0,\ i\in A.
		\label{eq:gaussian-singleton-criterion}
	\end{equation}
Equivalently, $K:=\Sigma^{-1}$ is an $M$-matrix, i.e.,
$K_{ij}\leq0$ for all $i\neq j$. More precisely,
$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(X_b\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$ is equivalent to
$\mathrm{dMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$ for nondegenerate Gaussian laws.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t:=(x_b-\mu_b-
	\boldsymbol\beta(\boldsymbol{x}_A-\boldsymbol\mu_A))/\sqrt v$
	and $\ell(t):=\log\Phi(t)$. Since
	$\ell''(t)<0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:gaussian-cmmtp2}
	gives
	$\partial_{ib}^2\log g
	=-\beta_i\ell''(t)/v\geq0$
	if and only if $\beta_i\geq0$.
	Moreover, for $i\neq j$, $i,j\in A$,
	$\partial_{ij}^2\log g
	=-S_{ij}+\beta_i\beta_j\ell''(t)/v$.
	As $t\to-\infty$, $\ell''(t)\to-1$, whereas
	$\ell''(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.
	Consequently, under $\boldsymbol\beta\geq\mathbf0$,
	the required condition is
	$S_{ij}+\beta_i\beta_j/v\leq0$.
	By the block inverse identity,
	$K_{AA}=S+\boldsymbol\beta^\top
	\boldsymbol\beta/v$ and
	$K_{Ab}=-\boldsymbol\beta^\top/v$.
	Hence the conditions are equivalent to
	$K_{ij}\leq0$ for all $i\neq j$.

\label{rem:gaussian-galambos}
	\begin{enumerate}
		\noindent\item[(i)]
		Let $\boldsymbol{U}$ have a $d$-dimensional Gaussian copula with correlation matrix $R$. If $R^{-1}$ is an $M$-matrix, i.e.,

label: ex:clayton-numerical
title: \bf Example
body_md:
\label{ex:clayton-numerical}
	Let $\boldsymbol{U}=(U_1,U_2,U_3)$ have the trivariate Clayton copula with parameter $\theta=2$, and take $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{3\}$. Then
	$\psi(t)=(1+t)^{-1/2}$ and
	$\varphi(u)=u^{-2}-1$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:clayton-cmmtp2},
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(U_3\mid(U_1,U_2))$ holds. We illustrate the
	corresponding lattice inequality in two steps.
	
	\textit{(i)}
	Since $|A|=2$,
	$h_2(t)=\psi''(t)=\frac{3}{4}(1+t)^{-5/2}$ and
	$-\varphi'(u)=2u^{-3}$. Hence, by
	\eqref{eq:archimedean-conditional-map},
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			g(u_1,u_2,u_3)
			&:=
			\mathbb P(U_3\leq u_3\mid U_1=u_1,U_2=u_2)c_A(u_1,u_2)=
			3u_1^{-3}u_2^{-3}
			\left(u_1^{-2}+u_2^{-2}+u_3^{-2}-2\right)^{-5/2}.
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:clayton-numerical-g}
	\end{equation}
	Moreover,
	$(\log h_2)''(t)=\frac{5}{2}(1+t)^{-2}>0$; thus
	Theorem~\ref{thm:archimedean-cmmtp2} yields
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(U_3\mid(U_1,U_2))$.
	
	\textit{(ii)}
	Choose $\boldsymbol{u}=(0.3,0.7,0.4)$ and
	$\boldsymbol{v}=(0.7,0.3,0.6)$. Then $\boldsymbol{u}\wedge\boldsymbol{v}=(0.3,0.3,0.4)$, and
	$\boldsymbol{u}\vee\boldsymbol{v}=(0.7,0.7,0.6)$. From
	\eqref{eq:clayton-numerical-g},
	\[
	\begin{array}{c|cccc}
		\boldsymbol{w}
		& \boldsymbol{u} & \boldsymbol{v} & \boldsymbol{u}\wedge\boldsymbol{v} & \boldsymbol{u}\vee\boldsymbol{v}\\ \hline
		g(\boldsymbol{w})
		&0.2564&0.4473&1.1413&0.4899
	\end{array}
	\]
	and therefore,
	\begin{equation}
		g(\boldsymbol{u})g(\boldsymbol{v})
		\approx(0.2564)(0.4473)
		=0.1147
		<
		0.5591
		=(1.1413)(0.4899)
		\approx
		g(\boldsymbol{u}\wedge\boldsymbol{v})g(\boldsymbol{u}\vee\boldsymbol{v}).
		\label{eq:clayton-numerical-lattice}
	\end{equation}
	Thus the $\mathrm{MTP}_2$ inequality for the conditional map is strict at this pair of noncomparable points, consistently with
	Theorem~\ref{thm:archimedean-cmmtp2}.

body_md:
\label{thm:closed-copula-representation}
	Let $A\dot\cup B=[d]$, $A,B\neq\varnothing$, and
	$\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}\sim C_n$, $\boldsymbol{U}\sim C$, where $C_n,C$ are
	$d$-copulas. If $C_n\to C$ on $[0,1]^d$ and
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B^{(n)}\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A^{(n)})$, $n\geq1$, then
	$\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{U}$ and
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)$. Moreover, for continuous
	strictly increasing distribution functions $F_i$, $i\in[d]$, with
	$Q_i:=F_i^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}:=Q(\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)})$ and
	$\boldsymbol{X}:=Q(\boldsymbol{U})$ satisfy
	$\boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{X}$ and
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(X_B\mid X_A)$.
head: environment

label: eq:copula-approx-lattice
title: Proof
body_md:
Define $\gamma_n:=\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}}$ and
	$\gamma:=\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol{U}}$. Since $C$ is a copula, it is continuous on $[0,1]^d$. Moreover,
	$\gamma_n([0,\boldsymbol{u}])=C_n(\boldsymbol{u})\to C(\boldsymbol{u})=\gamma([0,\boldsymbol{u}])$ for every
	$\boldsymbol{u}\in[0,1]^d$. Hence, the distribution-function characterization of weak convergence yields
	$\gamma_n\Rightarrow\gamma$ \citep{Billingsley1999}. Fix $\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B\in[0,1]^B$ and admissible
	$E,F\in\mathcal B([0,1]^A)$. For $n\geq1$, insert
	$\alpha_n(E):=\gamma_n(E\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B})$,
	$\beta_n(F):=\gamma_n(F\times L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B})$,
	$\alpha_n^\wedge(E\wedge F):=
	\gamma_n((E\wedge F)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B})$, and
	$\alpha_n^\vee(E\vee F):=
	\gamma_n((E\vee F)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B})$.
	Since
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B^{(n)}\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A^{(n)})$,
	Definition~\ref{def:conditional-measure-mtp2} gives
	\begin{equation}
		\alpha_n(E)\beta_n(F)
		\leq
		\alpha_n^{\wedge}(E\wedge F)
		\alpha_n^{\vee}(E\vee F).
		\label{eq:copula-approx-lattice}
	\end{equation}
	By $\gamma_n\Rightarrow\gamma$ and
	Theorem~\ref{thm:cmmtp2-weak-closure}, the weak limit inherits the
	conditional measure-theoretic lattice inequality. Therefore, for each admissible $E,F$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_B,\boldsymbol{y}_B$,
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{split}
			&\gamma(E\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B})
			\gamma(F\times L_{\boldsymbol{y}_B})\leq
			\gamma((E\wedge F)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\wedge\boldsymbol{y}_B})
			\gamma((E\vee F)\times L_{\boldsymbol{x}_B\vee\boldsymbol{y}_B}).
		\end{split}
		\label{eq:copula-limit-lattice}
	\end{equation}
	Hence, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)$ by Definition~\ref{def:conditional-measure-mtp2}. For the second assertion, define $Q(\boldsymbol{u}):=(Q_i(u_i))_{i\in[d]}$. Since the marginals of every copula are uniform,
	$\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}\in(0,1)^d)
	=\mathbb P(\boldsymbol{U}\in(0,1)^d)=1$. Each $Q_i$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $(0,1)$; hence the continuous mapping theorem
	gives $\boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}=Q(\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)})\Rightarrow Q(\boldsymbol{U})=\boldsymbol{X}$.
	Furthermore, for $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in(0,1)^d$,
	\begin{equation}
		Q(\boldsymbol{u}\wedge\boldsymbol{v})=Q(\boldsymbol{u})\wedge Q(\boldsymbol{v}),
		\qquad
		Q(\boldsymbol{u}\vee\boldsymbol{v})=Q(\boldsymbol{u})\vee Q(\boldsymbol{v}).
		\label{eq:quantile-lattice}
	\end{equation}
	Therefore, $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)$ and
	Theorem~\ref{thm:monotone-transformations} imply
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(X_B\mid X_A)$. This completes the proof.

label: cor:copula-whole-vector-closure
title: \bf Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:copula-whole-vector-closure}
	Let $\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}\sim C_n$, $\boldsymbol{U}\sim C$, where $C_n,C$ are	$d$-copulas and $C_n\to C$ on $[0,1]^d$. If
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)})$ holds for every $n\geq1$, then	$\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{U}$ and $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U})$. Moreover,
	if $F_i$, $i\in[d]$, are continuous and strictly increasing, $Q_i:=F_i^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}:=Q(\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)})$, and
	$\boldsymbol{X}:=Q(\boldsymbol{U})$, then $\boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{X}$ and $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $\varnothing\neq A\subsetneq[d]$, define $B:=[d]\setminus A$. Definition~\ref{def:cmmtp2-vector} yields
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B^{(n)}\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A^{(n)})$, $n\geq1$. Theorem~\ref{thm:closed-copula-representation} therefore yields $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}_B\mid\boldsymbol{U}_A)$ and $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(X_B\mid X_A)$ for every such $(A,B)$, together with $\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{U}$ and
	$\boldsymbol{X}^{(n)}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{X}$. Definition~\ref{def:cmmtp2-vector} now implies
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U})$ and $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X})$.

label: ex:singular-copula-limit
title: \bf Example
body_md:
\label{ex:singular-copula-limit}
	Let $\rho_n:=1-n^{-1}$, $n\geq2$, and let
	$\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}=(U_1^{(n)},U_2^{(n)})$ have the Gaussian copula
	$C_{\rho_n}$ with correlation matrix
	\[
	R_n=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		1&\rho_n\\
		\rho_n&1
	\end{pmatrix}.
	\]
	Let $M(u,v):=u\wedge v$ be the comonotonic copula. Then $C_{\rho_n}\to M$ pointwise on $[0,1]^2$ and
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)})$ holds for every $n\geq2$. We verify the limiting conclusion in two steps.
	
	\textit{(i)}
	For $\rho_n\in(0,1)$,
	\[
	R_n^{-1}
	=
	\frac{1}{1-\rho_n^2}
	\begin{pmatrix}
		1&-\rho_n\\
		-\rho_n&1
	\end{pmatrix},
	\]
	which is an $M$-matrix. Hence the corresponding Gaussian law is $\mathrm{dMTP}_2$ and, by Remark~\ref{rem:gaussian-galambos},
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)})$ holds. Moreover,
	$C_{\rho_n}$ is absolutely continuous on $(0,1)^2$ for every $n\geq2$.
	
	\textit{(ii)}
	Let $(Z_1^{(n)},Z_2^{(n)})\sim N(\mathbf 0,R_n)$ and define $U_i^{(n)}:=\Phi(Z_i^{(n)})$. Since
	$\rho_n\uparrow1$, $(Z_1^{(n)},Z_2^{(n)})\Rightarrow(Z,Z)$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and
	therefore,
	\[
	\boldsymbol{U}^{(n)}
	\Rightarrow
	(\Phi(Z),\Phi(Z))
	=:(U,U).
	\]
	The law $\gamma_M$ of $(U,U)$ is concentrated on
	$\Delta:=\{(u,u):0\leq u\leq1\}$, so that
	$\gamma_M(\Delta)=1$ whereas $\lambda^2(\Delta)=0$. Hence,
	$\gamma_M\perp\lambda^2$. Nevertheless,
	Corollary~\ref{cor:copula-whole-vector-closure} yields $\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(U,U)$. For example, at $(u,v)=(1/2,1/2)$,
	\[
	C_{\rho_n}(1/2,1/2)
	=
	\frac14+\frac{1}{2\pi}\arcsin(\rho_n)
	\longrightarrow
	\frac12
	=
	M(1/2,1/2).
	\]
	Therefore, a sequence of absolutely continuous
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2$ copulas converges to the singular comonotonic copula while the measure theoretic conditional total-positivity property is retained.

title: \bf Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:delta-lattice-expansion
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\boldsymbol{Z}^{(\ell)}\in\{0,1\}^{4m}$ are i.i.d. with
	$\mathbb E\boldsymbol{Z}^{(\ell)}=\boldsymbol{p}$ and
	$\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{Z}^{(\ell)})=\Sigma$, the multivariate central limit theorem yields
	$\sqrt n(\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n-\boldsymbol{p})\Rightarrow
	N_{4m}(\mathbf0,\Sigma)$ and hence,
	$\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n-\boldsymbol{p}=O_p(n^{-1/2})$.
	Put $\boldsymbol{h}_n:=\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n-\boldsymbol{p}$. For $r\in[m]$, direct expansion of
	$G_r$ gives
	\begin{equation}
		G_r(\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{h}_n)-G_r(\boldsymbol{p})
		=
		\nabla G_r(\boldsymbol{p})^\top\boldsymbol{h}_n
		+h_{n,r3}h_{n,r4}-h_{n,r1}h_{n,r2}.
		\label{eq:delta-lattice-expansion}
	\end{equation}
	Since $\boldsymbol{h}_n=O_p(n^{-1/2})$, the last two terms in
	\eqref{eq:delta-lattice-expansion} are $O_p(n^{-1})$.
	As $m<\infty$,
	$\sqrt n\{G(\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n)-G(\boldsymbol{p})\}
	=J(\boldsymbol{p})\sqrt n(\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n-\boldsymbol{p})+o_p(1)$.
	Slutsky's theorem therefore yields
	$
	\sqrt n\{G(\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n)-G(\boldsymbol{p})\}
	\Rightarrow
	N_m(\mathbf0,J(\boldsymbol{p})\Sigma J(\boldsymbol{p})^\top).
	$
	Since, $G(\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n)=\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_n$,
	$G(\boldsymbol{p})=\boldsymbol\Delta$, and
	$\Omega=J(\boldsymbol{p})\Sigma J(\boldsymbol{p})^\top$, \eqref{eq:lattice-contrast-clt}
	follows.

label: cor:lattice-contrast-studentization
title: \bf Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the law of large numbers,
	$\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n\stackrel{p}{\to}\boldsymbol{p}$ and
	$\widehat\Sigma_n\stackrel{p}{\to}\Sigma$.
	Continuity of $J$ gives
	$J(\widehat\boldsymbol{p}_n)\stackrel{p}{\to}J(\boldsymbol{p})$. Hence,
	$\widehat\Omega_n\stackrel{p}{\to}
	J(\boldsymbol{p})\Sigma J(\boldsymbol{p})^\top=\Omega$.
	Thus $\widehat\sigma_{n,r}\stackrel{p}{\to}\sigma_r>0$, and
	\eqref{eq:studentized-lattice-contrast} follows from
	Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-contrast-clt} and Slutsky's theorem.

label: prop:simultaneous-test
title: \bf Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $I_0:=\{r\in[m]:\Delta_r=0\}$. Under $H_0$, for
	$r\notin I_0$, $\sqrt n\,\widehat\Delta_{n,r}/
	\widehat\sigma_{n,r}\stackrel{p}{\to}\infty$, whereas, by Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-contrast-clt} and Corollary~\ref{cor:lattice-contrast-studentization},
	$(\sqrt n\,\widehat\Delta_{n,r}/\widehat\sigma_{n,r})_{r\in I_0}$ converges to the corresponding subvector of $Z\sim
	N_m(\mathbf0,R)$. Hence the asymptotic rejection probability is bounded by that obtained when $I_0=[m]$, i.e., $\boldsymbol\Delta=\mathbf0$. Since, $\widehat R_n\stackrel{p}{\to}R$,
	$c_{1-\alpha}(\widehat R_n)\stackrel{p}{\to}
	c_{1-\alpha}(R)$, and the assumed continuity at
	$c_{1-\alpha}(R)$ yields (i). If $I_0=[m]$, the bound is attained, which gives (ii). If $\Delta_{r_0}<0$ for some $r_0$, then
	$\sqrt n[-\widehat\Delta_{n,r_0}]_+/
	\widehat\sigma_{n,r_0}\stackrel{p}{\to}\infty$.
	Therefore, $T_n\stackrel{p}{\to}\infty$, whereas
	$c_{1-\alpha}(\widehat R_n)\stackrel{p}{\to}
	c_{1-\alpha}(R)<\infty$, proving (iii).

label: thm:local-power
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:local-power}
	Let $(\mu_n)$ be a sequence of laws with lattice contrasts
	$\boldsymbol\Delta_n$ and suppose
	$\sqrt n(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_n-\boldsymbol\Delta_n)
	\Rightarrow N_m(\mathbf0,\Omega)$,
	$\sqrt n\,\boldsymbol\Delta_n\to\boldsymbol\delta\in\mathbb{R}^m$, and
	$\widehat\Omega_n\stackrel{p}{\to}\Omega$, where
	$\sigma_r^2:=\Omega_{rr}>0$, $r\in[m]$. Let
	$D:=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ and
	$R:=D^{-1}\Omega D^{-1}$. Then
	\begin{equation}
		T_n\Rightarrow
		T(\boldsymbol\delta):=
		\max_{r\in[m]}
		\left[-Z_r-\frac{\delta_r}{\sigma_r}\right]_+,
		\quad
		\boldsymbol{Z}\sim N_m(\mathbf0,R).
		\label{eq:local-power}
	\end{equation}
	If the distribution of $T(\boldsymbol\delta)$ is continuous at
	$c_{1-\alpha}(R)$, then
	$\mathbb P_{\mu_n}(\varphi_n=1)\to
	\mathbb P\{T(\boldsymbol\delta)>c_{1-\alpha}(R)\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\widehat D_n:=
	\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_{n,1},\ldots,
	\widehat\sigma_{n,m})$. Since
	$\widehat\Omega_n\stackrel{p}{\to}\Omega$ and
	$\min_{r\in[m]}\sigma_r^2>0$,
	$\widehat D_n\stackrel{p}{\to}D$. Furthermore,
	\[
	\widehat D_n^{-1}\sqrt n\,\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_n
	=
	\widehat D_n^{-1}
	\sqrt n(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_n-\boldsymbol\Delta_n)
	+
	\widehat D_n^{-1}\sqrt n\,\boldsymbol\Delta_n
	\Rightarrow
	\boldsymbol{Z}+D^{-1}\boldsymbol\delta,
	\]
	by Slutsky's theorem. Since
	$\boldsymbol{z}\mapsto\max_{r\in[m]}[-z_r]_+$ is continuous,
	the continuous mapping theorem yields
	\eqref{eq:local-power}. Moreover,
	$\widehat R_n\stackrel{p}{\to}R$ implies
	$c_{1-\alpha}(\widehat R_n)\stackrel{p}{\to}
	c_{1-\alpha}(R)$. Continuity of the distribution of
	$T(\boldsymbol\delta)$ at $c_{1-\alpha}(R)$ therefore yields
	$\mathbb P_{\mu_n}(\varphi_n=1)\to
	\mathbb P\{T(\boldsymbol\delta)>c_{1-\alpha}(R)\}$.

label: ex:simultaneous-lattice-test
title: \bf Example
body_md:
\label{ex:simultaneous-lattice-test}
	Let $n=500$, $m=2$, and suppose the empirical probabilities associated
	with two comparisons in $\mathcal Q$ yield
	$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_n=(-0.020,0.008)^\top$ and
	$\widehat\Omega_n=\operatorname{diag}(0.0400,0.0256)$.
	Thus
	$\widehat\sigma_{n,1}=0.20$,
	$\widehat\sigma_{n,2}=0.16$, and $\widehat R_n=I_2$. From
	\eqref{eq:max-lattice-test},
	\[
	T_n
	=
	\max\left\{
	\frac{\sqrt{500}(0.020)}{0.20},
	0
	\right\}
	=2.236.
	\]
	For $\alpha=0.05$ and $\boldsymbol{Z}\sim N_2(\mathbf0,I_2)$,
	$c_{0.95}(I_2)=\Phi^{-1}(\sqrt{0.95})\approx1.955$.
	Hence $T_n>c_{0.95}(I_2)$ and $H_0$ is rejected. The first comparison
	therefore provides evidence of a lattice violation within
	$\mathcal Q$. This conclusion concerns the selected finite system and
	does not, by itself, constitute an omnibus test of
	$\mathrm{cmMTP}_2(\boldsymbol{X}_B\mid\boldsymbol{X}_A)$.
